title: Mathematical tools for models
audience: High school to early college bridge: learners comfortable with algebra, functions and basic probability
intro: Build the mathematics that causal and quantum models are written in: complex numbers and phase, vectors and inner products, matrices, tensor products and eigenvectors, derivatives and gradients, expectation, entropy, optimization, and estimation from data. Each idea is shown moving, stated carefully, proved where the proof is short, and checked in code. A correct calculation does not by itself show that a model describes a real system.

lessons.title: Complex numbers and phase
lessons.objective: Compute the modulus, argument, conjugate and polar form of a complex number, and explain why multiplication by a unit complex number is a rotation.
lessons.big_idea: A complex number is an arrow with a length and an angle; multiplying arrows multiplies lengths and adds angles, and that is why phase can make quantities cancel.
outcomes: Compute $|z|$, $\arg z$ and $\bar z$ for a complex number, and convert between $a + bi$ and $r e^{i\theta}$.
Explain multiplication by $e^{i\theta}$ as a rotation that keeps length, using Euler's formula.
Show that $|1 + e^{i\varphi}|^2 = 2 + 2\cos\varphi$ and say what it means for two equal-size contributions in and out of step.

key_terms.meaning: The plane whose horizontal axis is the real part and whose vertical axis is the imaginary part of a number $a + bi$.
The length $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ of the arrow from 0 to $z$.
The angle $\theta$ from the positive real axis to the arrow, defined up to whole turns of $2\pi$.
$\bar z = a - bi$, the reflection of $z = a + bi$ in the real axis.
$z = r e^{i\theta}$ with $r = |z|$ and $\theta = \arg z$.

motivation: Two waves of the same size can add to something twice as large or cancel to nothing. Ordinary positive numbers cannot do that, because adding positive amounts never gives zero. Complex numbers can, because each one carries an angle as well as a size.

Quantum theory writes every amplitude as a complex number. The probability of an outcome uses only the squared length, but the angles decide how amplitudes combine before that square is taken. This lesson builds the arithmetic you need for every later level: lengths, angles, conjugates and rotations.

blocks.md: Write a complex number as $z = a + bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real and $i^2 = -1$. Plot it at the point $(a, b)$, or think of it as the arrow from $0$ to that point. Adding complex numbers adds arrows head to tail, exactly like adding vectors in [L2-09](#lesson-l2-09).

blocks.title: Modulus, argument and conjugate
blocks.label: def-l3-01-modulus
blocks.md: For $z = a + bi$, the **modulus** is $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, an **argument** is any angle $\theta$ with $\cos\theta = a/|z|$ and $\sin\theta = b/|z|$, and the **conjugate** is $\bar z = a - bi$.

blocks.alt: The point z = 3 + 4i on a complex plane, its arrow of length 5, the angle of about 53 degrees, and its mirror image 3 - 4i.
blocks.caption: One number, three views: coordinates $3 + 4i$, length and angle, and the polar form $5e^{i\,0.927}$.
blocks.describe: The animation marks $z = 3 + 4i$, draws the legs 3 and 4 and the arrow, and computes $|z| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$. It shows the angle $\theta = \arctan(4/3) \approx 53.13^\circ$. It then reflects the arrow in the real axis to get $\bar z = 3 - 4i$ and multiplies: $z\bar z = 9 + 16 = 25 = |z|^2$. Finally it writes the same point as $z = 5e^{i\,0.927}$, length 5 and angle 0.927 radians.

blocks.latex: z\,\bar z = (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2
blocks.label: eq-l3-01-zzbar

blocks.md: Equation [](#eq-l3-01-zzbar) is the most used identity in this course. For $z = 3 + 4i$ it gives $z\bar z = 9 + 16 = 25$, so $|z| = 5$. The angle is $\arctan(4/3) \approx 53.13^\circ$, or $0.927$ radians.

blocks.title: Euler's formula
blocks.label: thm-l3-01-euler
blocks.md: For every real $\theta$, $\; e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$.

Compare power series. $e^{x} = \sum_{k \ge 0} x^k / k!$ converges for every complex $x$. Put $x = i\theta$ and use $i^2 = -1$, $i^3 = -i$, $i^4 = 1$. The even terms give $1 - \theta^2/2! + \theta^4/4! - \dots = \cos\theta$, and the odd terms give $i(\theta - \theta^3/3! + \dots) = i\sin\theta$.

So every complex number can be written $z = r e^{i\theta}$ with $r = |z|$. In polar form multiplication is easy: $r_1 e^{i\theta_1} \cdot r_2 e^{i\theta_2} = r_1 r_2\, e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}$. Lengths multiply and angles add [@openstax_polar].

blocks.title: Multiplying by a unit number is a rotation
blocks.md: If $|w| = 1$, then $w = e^{i\alpha}$ and $wz$ has the same length as $z$, turned by $\alpha$. Multiplying by $i = e^{i\pi/2}$ is a quarter turn: $i(2 + i) = -1 + 2i$.

blocks.caption: Repeated multiplication by $w = e^{2\pi i/n}$ walks around the unit circle in equal steps. After $n$ steps it returns to 1, so these points solve $z^n = 1$.

blocks.caption: Multiplication by $i$ turns the plane; then the sum $1 + e^{i\varphi}$ swings from length 2 to 0 and back as $\varphi$ goes once around.
blocks.describe: First the arrow $z = 2 + i$ rotates by a quarter turn into $iz = -1 + 2i$, keeping its length, because $i = e^{i\pi/2}$. Then a blue arrow 1 and an orange arrow $e^{i\varphi}$ are placed head to tail, with their red sum. As $\varphi$ sweeps from 0 to $2\pi$, a graph traces the squared length of the sum, $2 + 2\cos\varphi$: it is 4 when the arrows point the same way and 0 when they point opposite ways.

blocks.caption: Drag the slider to change the relative phase $\varphi$. The red point on the right is the squared length of the red sum arrow on the left.
blocks.describe: The first panel shows the arrows $1$ and $e^{i\varphi}$ head to tail and their sum. The second panel plots $|1 + e^{i\varphi}|^2 = 2 + 2\cos\varphi$ for $\varphi$ from $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$, with a marker at the chosen phase: 4 at $0^\circ$, 2 at $90^\circ$, 0 at $180^\circ$.

blocks.md: In step ($\varphi = 0$) the squared length is 4, twice the sum of the separate squared lengths. Opposite ($\varphi = \pi$) it is 0. On average over $\varphi$ it is 2, the same as adding the squared lengths. This is the arithmetic behind interference, which [L5-03](#lesson-l5-03) uses for quantum amplitudes.

blocks.explain: Python has complex numbers built in (`1j` is $i$), and `cmath` gives modulus and argument. Run the cell and change `z`.
blocks.source:
import cmath

z = 3 + 4j
r, theta = abs(z), cmath.phase(z)
print('modulus', r, ' argument (rad)', round(theta, 3))
print('conjugate', z.conjugate(), ' z * conj(z) =', z * z.conjugate())
print('polar back to Cartesian:', cmath.rect(r, theta))

# multiplying by i is a quarter turn
w = 2 + 1j
print('i * (2 + i) =', 1j * w, ' same length:', abs(w), abs(1j * w))

# |1 + e^{i phi}|^2 = 2 + 2 cos(phi)
for deg in (0, 90, 180):
    phi = cmath.pi * deg / 180
    print(deg, round(abs(1 + cmath.exp(1j * phi)) ** 2, 6), round(2 + 2 * cmath.cos(phi).real, 6))

blocks.title: Why the argument needs care
blocks.md: The angle is defined only up to adding $2\pi$. Software returns a principal value in $(-\pi, \pi]$; `cmath.phase(-1)` is $\pi$, and `cmath.phase(-1-1e-17j)` is close to $-\pi$. Differences of phases are what matter physically.

worked_example.title: From coordinates to polar form and back
worked_example.problem: Let $z = -1 + i\sqrt{3}$. Find $|z|$, $\arg z$, the polar form, and $z^3$.
steps: Modulus: $|z| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (\sqrt3)^2} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.
Argument: the point is in the second quadrant with $\cos\theta = -1/2$ and $\sin\theta = \sqrt3/2$, so $\theta = 2\pi/3$ ($120^\circ$).
Polar form: $z = 2e^{2\pi i/3}$.
Power: $z^3 = 2^3 e^{3 \cdot 2\pi i/3} = 8e^{2\pi i} = 8$. Check by expanding $(-1 + i\sqrt3)^2 = -2 - 2i\sqrt3$, then multiplying by $-1 + i\sqrt3$ to get $8$.
worked_example.result: $z = 2e^{2\pi i/3}$ and $z^3 = 8$: cubing multiplies the length by itself three times and triples the angle.

exercises.prompt: For $z = 5 - 12i$, find $|z|$, $\bar z$ and $z\bar z$.
Write $z = 1 + i$ in polar form and compute $z^8$.
exercises.solution: $|z| = \sqrt2$ and $\arg z = \pi/4$, so $z = \sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}$. Then $z^8 = (\sqrt2)^8 e^{2\pi i} = 16$.

exercises.prompt: Show that $|zw| = |z||w|$ for any complex $z, w$ using only $|u|^2 = u\bar u$.
exercises.solution: $|zw|^2 = zw\,\overline{zw} = zw\,\bar z\bar w = (z\bar z)(w\bar w) = |z|^2|w|^2$, and moduli are non-negative, so $|zw| = |z||w|$.

exercises.prompt: For which phases $\varphi$ is $|1 + e^{i\varphi}|^2$ equal to 1? What fraction of the in-step value is that?
exercises.solution: $2 + 2\cos\varphi = 1$ gives $\cos\varphi = -1/2$, so $\varphi = 2\pi/3$ or $4\pi/3$. That is $1/4$ of the in-step value 4.

exercises.prompt: Add $n$ unit arrows with angles $0, \varphi, 2\varphi, \dots, (n-1)\varphi$. Show that the squared length of the sum is $\sin^2(n\varphi/2)/\sin^2(\varphi/2)$ when $\varphi$ is not a multiple of $2\pi$.
exercises.solution: The sum is a geometric series: $S = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} e^{ik\varphi} = (e^{in\varphi} - 1)/(e^{i\varphi} - 1)$. Use $e^{ix} - 1 = e^{ix/2}\,2i\sin(x/2)$ for numerator and denominator. The phases have modulus 1, so $|S| = |\sin(n\varphi/2)|/|\sin(\varphi/2)|$. For $n = 2$ this gives $\sin^2\varphi/\sin^2(\varphi/2) = 4\cos^2(\varphi/2) = 2 + 2\cos\varphi$, matching [](#eq-l3-01-sum).

check.question: What is $z\bar z$ for $z = 3 + 4i$?
What does multiplying a complex number by $e^{i\pi/3}$ do to its arrow?
options: Reflects it in the real axis
Turns it by $60^\circ$ and keeps its length
check.explanation: $|e^{i\pi/3}| = 1$, and angles add under multiplication, so the arrow turns by $\pi/3 = 60^\circ$ with its length unchanged.

check.question: Two unit arrows point in exactly opposite directions. What is the squared length of their sum?
check.explanation: Opposite directions means $\varphi = \pi$, and $2 + 2\cos\pi = 0$: the arrows cancel.

check.question: A two-outcome state vector has amplitudes $(\cos t, \sin t)$. What do the chances of the two outcomes add to?
check.explanation: The chances are $\cos^2 t$ and $\sin^2 t$, and $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$ for every $t$. Complex amplitudes keep this rule with $|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$.

misconceptions.claim: "$i$ is imaginary, so it is not a real tool."
misconceptions.correction: $i$ is just the number whose square is $-1$. Geometrically it is a quarter turn, and it makes rotations and waves easy to compute.

misconceptions.claim: "Phase does not matter because probabilities only use $|z|^2$."
misconceptions.correction: The phase of one number alone does not change $|z|^2$, but the relative phase of two numbers changes $|z_1 + z_2|^2$ from $(|z_1| + |z_2|)^2$ down to $(|z_1| - |z_2|)^2$.

misconceptions.claim: "The argument of $z$ is $\arctan(b/a)$."
misconceptions.correction: That formula loses the quadrant: $-1 - i$ and $1 + i$ give the same ratio. Use both $\cos\theta = a/|z|$ and $\sin\theta = b/|z|$ (the two-argument arctangent).

lessons.connect: Complex amplitudes and relative phase return in [L3-02](#lesson-l3-02) as inner products of complex vectors, and in quantum gates as unitary rotations. Up to normalization, the formula $2 + 2\cos\varphi$ is the interference pattern of the Mach-Zehnder interferometer.
lessons.caution: This lesson treats complex numbers as a mathematical tool. Saying that amplitudes are complex does not by itself explain any physical experiment; that needs the measurement rules of quantum theory introduced in Level 5.

instructor.why: Students meet complex numbers as algebra rules; quantum information needs them as geometry. Linking multiplication to rotation and conjugation to reflection makes later unitary and inner-product arguments visual [@openstax_polar; @feynman].
teaching_notes: Start from the in-step and opposite cases of two arrows before any formula; students predict 2 and 0 for the length, then check $4$ and $0$ for the squared length.
Insist on the two-argument arctangent; give $-1 - i$ as a test case.
Use the interactive figure to show that the average of $2 + 2\cos\varphi$ over a full turn is 2, the sum of the separate squared lengths.
instructor.assessment: Exercise 3 (multiplicativity of the modulus) and the challenge exercise show whether students can move between algebraic and geometric reasoning; the check questions test the core computations.
instructor.extend: Derive De Moivre's formula $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta$ and use it to find $\cos 3\theta$ in terms of $\cos\theta$. The Feynman Lectures, Volume III, chapter 1, uses arrows of this kind for amplitudes [@feynman].

lessons.title: Vectors and inner products
lessons.objective: Normalize a real or complex vector, compute inner products with the conjugate in the right place, and use an orthonormal basis to expand a vector and read off squared overlaps.
lessons.big_idea: The inner product measures how much of one vector lies along another: for a unit vector it is the signed length of a shadow, it never exceeds the product of the lengths, and for complex entries it needs a conjugate so that every nonzero vector has positive length.
outcomes: Compute $\|v\|$ and the normalized vector $v/\|v\|$ for real and complex vectors, and the inner product $\langle u, v\rangle = \sum_j \bar u_j v_j$.
Interpret $\langle u, v\rangle$ for a unit vector $u$ as the signed length of the shadow of $v$ on the line of $u$, and find the projection and the orthogonal remainder.
State and prove the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|\langle u, v\rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|$, and use it to define the angle between real vectors.
Expand a vector in an orthonormal basis, check $\sum_k |\langle e_k, v\rangle|^2 = \|v\|^2$, and say when a squared overlap can be read as a probability.

key_terms.meaning: The length $\|v\| = \sqrt{\langle v, v\rangle}$ of a vector; for real entries $\sqrt{v_1^2 + \dots + v_n^2}$, for complex entries $\sqrt{|v_1|^2 + \dots + |v_n|^2}$.
A vector of norm 1. Dividing a nonzero vector by its norm normalizes it without changing its direction.
$\langle u, v\rangle = \sum_j \bar u_j v_j$: conjugate the entries of the first vector, multiply entry by entry, add.
Two vectors with $\langle u, v\rangle = 0$.
For a unit vector $u$, the vector $\langle u, v\rangle\, u$: the part of $v$ that lies along $u$.
A basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of unit vectors that are pairwise orthogonal, $\langle e_j, e_k\rangle = \delta_{jk}$.

motivation: Here is a puzzle. The vector $(1, i)$ is clearly not the zero vector, yet if you compute its squared length the way you would for a real vector, $1^2 + i^2 = 1 - 1 = 0$. A length formula that gives zero for a nonzero vector is useless. Something has to change when vectors have complex entries, and the fix (one complex conjugate, placed in the right slot) is a convention that every later quantum lesson relies on.

The second reason to care is that almost every question you will ask about a state vector is an inner product. How much of this signal lies along that pattern? How similar are two word embeddings? What is the chance that a qubit prepared one way passes a test for another? Each answer is a number $\langle u, v\rangle$, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees that such numbers stay within the bounds the lengths allow. This lesson builds the picture first, a shadow on a line, and then the algebra that carries the picture into complex spaces.

blocks.md: A vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ or $\mathbb{C}^n$ is an ordered list of $n$ numbers. Each position names a basis direction, so the order matters. In two real dimensions a vector $v = (v_1, v_2)$ is an arrow from the origin to the point $(v_1, v_2)$, exactly as in [L2-09](#lesson-l2-09). We build every idea on that picture first and carry it to complex entries in the third section [@openstax_vectors; @mml].

blocks.title: Norm and normalization
blocks.label: def-l3-02-norm
blocks.md: The **norm** of $v \in \mathbb{C}^n$ is $\|v\| = \sqrt{|v_1|^2 + \dots + |v_n|^2}$. For real entries $|v_j|^2 = v_j^2$. A **unit vector** has norm 1. If $v \ne 0$, the vector $\hat v = v / \|v\|$ is the **normalization** of $v$: it points the same way and has norm 1.

For $v = (3, 4)$, equation [](#eq-l3-02-norm) gives $\|v\| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ and $\hat v = (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8)$. Check: $0.36 + 0.64 = 1$. Normalizing slides the tip of the arrow along its own line until it lands on the unit circle; the direction does not change because we divided by a positive number.

sections.heading: The dot product as a shadow

blocks.title: Dot product of real vectors
blocks.label: def-l3-02-dot
blocks.md: For $u, v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $\; u \cdot v = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + \dots + u_n v_n$. In particular $v \cdot v = \|v\|^2$.

The second equality in [](#eq-l3-02-dot), with $\theta$ the angle between the arrows, is the law of cosines in disguise: expand $\|v - u\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - 2\,u\cdot v$ and compare with $\|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - 2\|u\|\|v\|\cos\theta$. Its geometric reading is the key picture of this lesson. If $u$ is a **unit** vector, $u \cdot v = \|v\|\cos\theta$ is the signed length of the shadow that $v$ casts on the line through $u$ when light falls perpendicular to that line.

blocks.alt: The arrow v = (3, 4) of length 5 shrinks onto the unit circle at (0.6, 0.8); then it casts a shadow of length 4.8 on the line of the unit vector u = (0.8, 0.6), with a leftover piece of length 1.4 at right angles.
blocks.caption: Normalize, then project: $\hat v = (0.6, 0.8)$, and the shadow of $v = (3, 4)$ on $u = (0.8, 0.6)$ has length $\langle u, v\rangle = 4.8$.
blocks.describe: The animation draws $v = (3, 4)$ and computes $\|v\| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$. The arrow then shrinks along its own line onto the unit circle, ending at $\hat v = (0.6, 0.8)$. The full arrow returns and the unit vector $u = (0.8, 0.6)$ appears with the line through it. A dashed perpendicular drops from the tip of $v$ to that line; the shadow from the origin to the foot is highlighted and labeled $\langle u, v\rangle = 0.8 \cdot 3 + 0.6 \cdot 4 = 4.8$. The leftover piece from the foot to the tip of $v$ has length 1.4 and meets the line at a right angle, and the screen checks $4.8^2 + 1.4^2 = 25 = \|v\|^2$.

blocks.title: Projection on a unit vector
blocks.label: prop-l3-02-projection
blocks.md: Let $u$ be a unit vector and $v$ any vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Put $p = (u \cdot v)\,u$ and $r = v - p$. Then $u \cdot r = 0$ and $\|v\|^2 = (u\cdot v)^2 + \|r\|^2$.

$u \cdot r = u \cdot v - (u\cdot v)(u \cdot u) = u\cdot v - u \cdot v = 0$ because $u \cdot u = 1$. Since $p$ is a multiple of $u$, also $p \cdot r = 0$. Then $\|v\|^2 = (p + r)\cdot(p + r) = \|p\|^2 + 2\,p\cdot r + \|r\|^2 = (u\cdot v)^2 + \|r\|^2$.

With $v = (3, 4)$ and $u = (0.8, 0.6)$: $u \cdot v = 2.4 + 2.4 = 4.8$, the projection is $p = 4.8\,(0.8, 0.6) = (3.84, 2.88)$, and the remainder is $r = (-0.84, 1.12)$ with $\|r\| = 1.4$. The proposition says $4.8^2 + 1.4^2 = 25$, and indeed $23.04 + 1.96 = 25$. The angle between $u$ and $v$ satisfies $\cos\theta = 4.8/5 = 0.96$, so $\theta \approx 16.26^\circ$.

blocks.caption: Turn the unit vector $u$ with the slider. The shadow of $v = (3, 4)$ on the line of $u$ (left) has signed length $\langle u, v\rangle$, plotted on the right; it never leaves the band between $-5$ and $5$.
blocks.describe: The first panel shows $v = (3, 4)$, a unit vector $u$ at the chosen angle, the dashed line through $u$, the perpendicular from the tip of $v$, and the shadow from the origin to its foot. The second panel plots $\langle u, v\rangle = 5\cos(\alpha - 53.13^\circ)$ against the angle $\alpha$ of $u$, with dotted lines at $\pm 5$ and a marker at the chosen angle. The shadow is longest, 5, at $\alpha = 53.13^\circ$, zero at $143.13^\circ$ and $323.13^\circ$, and $-5$ at $233.13^\circ$.

blocks.md: Return to the puzzle: $(1, i)$ is not zero, yet $1\cdot 1 + i \cdot i = 0$. The cure is the identity $z\bar z = |z|^2$ from [L3-01](#lesson-l3-01). Conjugate the first vector's entries before multiplying: $\bar 1 \cdot 1 + \bar i \cdot i = 1 + (-i)(i) = 1 + 1 = 2$, so $\|(1, i)\| = \sqrt 2$.

blocks.title: The complex inner product
blocks.label: def-l3-02-inner
blocks.md: For $u, v \in \mathbb{C}^n$, $\; \langle u, v\rangle = \bar u_1 v_1 + \bar u_2 v_2 + \dots + \bar u_n v_n$. It has three properties: it is linear in the second slot, $\langle u, a v + b w\rangle = a\langle u, v\rangle + b\langle u, w\rangle$; it is conjugate symmetric, $\langle v, u\rangle = \overline{\langle u, v\rangle}$; and it is positive definite, $\langle v, v\rangle = \|v\|^2 \ge 0$ with equality only for $v = 0$. Together the first two give $\langle a u, v\rangle = \bar a\,\langle u, v\rangle$. For real vectors it is the dot product.

blocks.alt: A derivation shows that (1, i) has squared length 0 without the conjugate and 2 with it; then the overlap of (1, 1)/sqrt 2 with (1, e to the i phi)/sqrt 2 is drawn as an arrow in the complex plane whose squared length traces (1 + cos phi)/2.
blocks.caption: Why the conjugate is needed, and what a complex overlap looks like: $\langle u, v_\varphi\rangle = (1 + e^{i\varphi})/2$ has squared modulus $\frac{1 + \cos\varphi}{2}$.
blocks.describe: First the screen computes the squared length of $(1, i)$ without a conjugate, $1\cdot 1 + i\cdot i = 1 - 1 = 0$, and marks it as wrong for a nonzero vector. The line transforms term by term into the correct version $\bar 1 \cdot 1 + \bar i\cdot i = 1 + 1 = 2$. Next it takes $u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $v_\varphi = (1, e^{i\varphi})/\sqrt2$ and derives $\langle u, v_\varphi\rangle = \frac{1 + e^{i\varphi}}{2}$. In a complex plane on the left this overlap is drawn as an arrow from the origin; as $\varphi$ sweeps from 0 to $2\pi$ its tip goes around the circle of radius $1/2$ centered at $1/2$. On the right a graph traces $|\langle u, v_\varphi\rangle|^2 = \frac{1 + \cos\varphi}{2}$: 1 at $\varphi = 0$, $1/2$ at $\varphi = \pi/2$, and 0 at $\varphi = \pi$, where the vectors are orthogonal. Finally the screen notes $\langle v, u\rangle = \overline{\langle u, v\rangle}$: swapping the slots reflects the arrow in the real axis.

blocks.md: The overlap in the animation is the formula $|1 + e^{i\varphi}|^2 = 2 + 2\cos\varphi$ of [L3-01](#lesson-l3-01) divided by 4. The vectors $u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $v_\varphi = (1, e^{i\varphi})/\sqrt2$ have identical entry sizes; only the relative phase $\varphi$ differs, and that alone moves their squared overlap from 1 down to 0. For $\varphi = \pi/2$, $\langle u, v_\varphi\rangle = (1 + i)/2$ and $|(1 + i)/2|^2 = 1/2$.

blocks.title: Which slot gets the conjugate
blocks.md: Physics and quantum computing conjugate the **first** slot, as here; NumPy's `np.vdot(u, v)` does the same. Many mathematics texts conjugate the second slot instead. The two conventions give complex conjugate answers, so the modulus $|\langle u, v\rangle|$ and every probability are the same. In Level 5 the inner product is written $\langle u|v\rangle$ [@nielsenchuang; @watrous].

sections.heading: Cauchy-Schwarz: a shadow is never longer than the arrow

blocks.title: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
blocks.label: thm-l3-02-cs
blocks.md: For all $u, v \in \mathbb{C}^n$ (with the inner product of [](#eq-l3-02-inner)), $\; |\langle u, v\rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|$. Equality holds exactly when one of the vectors is a scalar multiple of the other.

If $u = 0$ both sides are 0, and $u = 0 = 0\cdot v$ is a multiple. Otherwise put $c = \langle u, v\rangle / \|u\|^2$, $p = c\,u$ and $r = v - p$. Then $\langle u, r\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle - c\langle u, u\rangle = 0$, and so $\langle p, r\rangle = \bar c\,\langle u, r\rangle = 0$. Expanding, $\|v\|^2 = \|p\|^2 + \|r\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle p, r\rangle = \|p\|^2 + \|r\|^2 \ge \|p\|^2 = |c|^2\|u\|^2 = |\langle u, v\rangle|^2/\|u\|^2$. Multiply by $\|u\|^2$ and take square roots. Equality forces $\|r\| = 0$, that is $v = c\,u$; conversely if $v = c\,u$ (or $u = c\,v$) both sides equal $|c|\,\|u\|^2$ (or $|c|\,\|v\|^2$).

For real nonzero vectors the theorem says $-1 \le \frac{u\cdot v}{\|u\|\|v\|} \le 1$, so we may **define** the angle between them by $\cos\theta = \frac{u\cdot v}{\|u\|\|v\|}$ with $0 \le \theta \le \pi$. This is how the angle between two vectors in 300 dimensions (two word embeddings, say) makes sense even though nobody can draw it. The same ratio is the cosine similarity used in machine learning [@mml].

blocks.title: Complex vectors have no single angle
blocks.md: For complex vectors $\langle u, v\rangle$ is a complex number, so the ratio $\langle u, v\rangle/(\|u\|\|v\|)$ is a point in the unit disk rather than a cosine. Its modulus, between 0 and 1, measures how parallel the vectors are; its phase is a relative phase of the kind studied in [L3-01](#lesson-l3-01).

blocks.title: Orthonormal basis
blocks.label: def-l3-02-onb
blocks.md: Vectors $e_1, \dots, e_n$ in $\mathbb{C}^n$ form an **orthonormal basis** if $\langle e_j, e_k\rangle = \delta_{jk}$ (1 when $j = k$, 0 otherwise). In $\mathbb{C}^2$ the standard basis, labeled from 0 as in quantum computing, $e_0 = (1, 0)$, $e_1 = (0, 1)$, is one; so is $e_\pm = (1, \pm 1)/\sqrt2$.

blocks.title: Coordinates are inner products (Parseval)
blocks.label: prop-l3-02-parseval
blocks.md: If $e_1, \dots, e_n$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{C}^n$, then every $v$ satisfies $v = \sum_k \langle e_k, v\rangle\, e_k$ and $\|v\|^2 = \sum_k |\langle e_k, v\rangle|^2$.

Because the $e_k$ form a basis, $v = \sum_k c_k e_k$ for some numbers $c_k$. Take the inner product with $e_j$ and use linearity in the second slot: $\langle e_j, v\rangle = \sum_k c_k \langle e_j, e_k\rangle = c_j$. Then $\|v\|^2 = \langle \sum_j c_j e_j, \sum_k c_k e_k\rangle = \sum_{j,k} \bar c_j c_k\,\delta_{jk} = \sum_k |c_k|^2$, using $\langle a u, w\rangle = \bar a\langle u, w\rangle$ in the first slot.

blocks.caption: One arrow, two orthonormal bases. In the standard basis $v = (3, 4)$; in the turned basis $u_1 = (0.8, 0.6)$, $u_2 = (-0.6, 0.8)$ its coordinates are the shadows $4.8$ and $1.4$. Both pairs satisfy $3^2 + 4^2 = 4.8^2 + 1.4^2 = 25$.

blocks.title: When is a squared overlap a probability?
blocks.md: In quantum theory, if $\psi$ is a **normalized** state vector and $e_1, \dots, e_n$ is the **orthonormal** basis of a measurement, the outcome $k$ has probability $|\langle e_k, \psi\rangle|^2$; Parseval guarantees these add to 1. Without normalization, or for vectors that are not orthonormal, squared overlaps need not add to 1 and are not probabilities. The physical rule is a postulate introduced in Level 5, not a consequence of the algebra here [@preskill].

blocks.explain: NumPy computes everything in this lesson. `np.dot` is the plain sum of products; `np.vdot` conjugates its first argument and is the inner product of [](#eq-l3-02-inner). The last loop tests Cauchy-Schwarz on 1000 random complex vectors.
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

# real vectors: length, normalization, shadow (projection) on a unit vector
v = np.array([3.0, 4.0])
u = np.array([0.8, 0.6])                      # a unit vector
norm_v = np.linalg.norm(v)
print('||v|| =', norm_v, '  v/||v|| =', v / norm_v)
shadow = np.dot(u, v)                         # = ||v|| cos(angle)
p = shadow * u                                # projection of v on the line of u
r = v - p                                     # what is left over
print('<u, v> =', round(shadow, 6), ' projection', p.round(4), ' residual', r.round(4))
print('residual is orthogonal to u:', round(float(np.dot(u, r)), 12))
print('Pythagoras 4.8^2 + 1.4^2 =', round(shadow**2 + np.dot(r, r), 10))
angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(shadow / (np.linalg.norm(u) * norm_v)))
print('angle between u and v (degrees):', round(angle, 2))

# complex vectors: np.vdot conjugates its FIRST argument
w = np.array([1, 1j])
print('naive sum of squares of (1, i):', np.sum(w * w), '  <w, w> =', np.vdot(w, w))
a, b = np.array([1, 1j]), np.array([1j, 1])
print('<a, b> =', np.vdot(a, b), '  plain dot =', np.dot(a, b), '  <b, a> =', np.vdot(b, a))

# orthonormal basis expansion (Parseval) for the worked example psi = (1 + i, 1)/sqrt(3)
psi = np.array([1 + 1j, 1]) / np.sqrt(3)
plus, minus = np.array([1, 1]) / np.sqrt(2), np.array([1, -1]) / np.sqrt(2)
c_plus, c_minus = np.vdot(plus, psi), np.vdot(minus, psi)
print('|<+, psi>|^2 =', round(abs(c_plus)**2, 6), '  |<-, psi>|^2 =', round(abs(c_minus)**2, 6))
assert abs(abs(c_plus)**2 - 5/6) < 1e-12 and abs(abs(c_minus)**2 - 1/6) < 1e-12
assert np.allclose(c_plus * plus + c_minus * minus, psi)

# Cauchy-Schwarz on random complex vectors (seeded)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
worst = 0.0
for _ in range(1000):
    x = rng.normal(size=4) + 1j * rng.normal(size=4)
    y = rng.normal(size=4) + 1j * rng.normal(size=4)
    worst = max(worst, abs(np.vdot(x, y)) / (np.linalg.norm(x) * np.linalg.norm(y)))
print('largest |<x,y>| / (||x|| ||y||) in 1000 random trials:', round(worst, 4), '(never above 1)')

worked_example.title: A complex state in two bases
worked_example.problem: Let $\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1 + i,\ 1)$. Check that $\psi$ is normalized, compute its overlaps with $e_\pm = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, \pm 1)$, and verify Parseval.
steps: Overlap with $e_+$: the entries of $e_+$ are real, so conjugating changes nothing: $\langle e_+, \psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left((1 + i) + 1\right) = \frac{2 + i}{\sqrt6}$, and $|\langle e_+, \psi\rangle|^2 = \frac{4 + 1}{6} = \frac56$.
Overlap with $e_-$: $\langle e_-, \psi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left((1 + i) - 1\right) = \frac{i}{\sqrt6}$, and $|\langle e_-, \psi\rangle|^2 = \frac16$.
Parseval: $\frac56 + \frac16 = 1 = \|\psi\|^2$. Reconstruction: $\frac{2 + i}{\sqrt6}\,e_+ + \frac{i}{\sqrt6}\,e_- = \frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\left(2 + 2i,\ 2\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1 + i, 1) = \psi$.
worked_example.result: $\psi$ is a unit vector with squared overlaps $5/6$ and $1/6$ on $e_+$ and $e_-$. If $\psi$ is a qubit state and $\{e_+, e_-\}$ the measurement basis, these are the outcome probabilities.

exercises.prompt: Normalize $v = (1, 1)$. Compute the squared overlap of the result with $e_1 = (0, 1)$.
exercises.solution: $\|v\| = \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt2$, so $\hat v = (1/\sqrt2, 1/\sqrt2)$. Then $\langle e_1, \hat v\rangle = 0\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2} + 1\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and the squared overlap is $\frac12$.

exercises.prompt: Find the angle between $u = (2, -1, 2)$ and $v = (1, 2, 2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
exercises.solution: $u\cdot v = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4$, $\|u\| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$, $\|v\| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$. So $\cos\theta = 4/9 \approx 0.444$ and $\theta = \arccos(4/9) \approx 63.61^\circ$.

exercises.prompt: Let $a = (1, i)$ and $b = (i, 1)$. Compute $\langle a, b\rangle$, $\langle b, a\rangle$ and the plain sum of products $a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2$. Are $a$ and $b$ orthogonal?
exercises.solution: $\langle a, b\rangle = \bar 1\cdot i + \bar i \cdot 1 = i - i = 0$, and $\langle b, a\rangle = \overline{0} = 0$ (directly: $\bar i\cdot 1 + \bar 1\cdot i = -i + i = 0$). The plain sum is $i + i = 2i$. With the correct inner product $a$ and $b$ are orthogonal, even though the naive formula suggests otherwise.

exercises.prompt: Express $v = (3, 4)$ in the orthonormal basis $u_1 = (0.8, 0.6)$, $u_2 = (-0.6, 0.8)$. Check that the basis is orthonormal and that Parseval holds.
Prove the triangle inequality $\|u + v\| \le \|u\| + \|v\|$ for $u, v \in \mathbb{C}^n$. When does equality hold?
exercises.solution: $\|u + v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 + \langle u, v\rangle + \langle v, u\rangle = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v\rangle$. Since $\operatorname{Re} z \le |z|$ and by Cauchy-Schwarz $|\langle u, v\rangle| \le \|u\|\|v\|$, this is at most $\|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 + 2\|u\|\|v\| = (\|u\| + \|v\|)^2$. Take square roots. Equality needs $\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v\rangle = \|u\|\|v\|$, which forces both $|\langle u, v\rangle| = \|u\|\|v\|$ (so one vector is a multiple of the other) and $\langle u, v\rangle$ real and non-negative: equality holds exactly when one vector is a non-negative real multiple of the other.

exercises.prompt: Let $u$ be a unit vector in $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $v$ any vector. Show that $\|v - c\,u\|^2$ over complex $c$ is smallest at $c = \langle u, v\rangle$, with minimum value $\|v\|^2 - |\langle u, v\rangle|^2$. Evaluate it for $v = (3, 4)$ and $u = (0.8, 0.6)$.
exercises.solution: Write $s = \langle u, v\rangle$. Expanding, $\|v - c u\|^2 = \|v\|^2 - \bar c\, s - c\,\bar s + |c|^2 = \|v\|^2 - |s|^2 + |c - s|^2$, since $|c - s|^2 = |c|^2 - c\bar s - \bar c s + |s|^2$. The last term is $\ge 0$ and vanishes only at $c = s$, so the minimum is $\|v\|^2 - |s|^2$. For the example $s = 4.8$ and the minimum is $25 - 23.04 = 1.96$, a distance of $1.4$: the length of the remainder in the projection picture.

check.question: What is the normalization of $v = (3, 4)$?
check.explanation: $\|v\| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$, so $v/\|v\| = (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8)$, which has norm $\sqrt{0.36 + 0.64} = 1$. Dividing by the sum of entries, 7, does not give a unit vector.

check.question: For $a = (1, i)$ and $b = (i, 1)$, what is $\langle a, b\rangle = \bar a_1 b_1 + \bar a_2 b_2$?
check.explanation: $\bar 1\cdot i + \bar i\cdot 1 = i + (-i) = 0$, so the vectors are orthogonal. Forgetting the conjugate gives $2i$.

check.question: Real vectors $u$ and $v$ have $\|u\| = 1$ and $\|v\| = 5$. Which value is impossible for $u\cdot v$?
check.explanation: By Cauchy-Schwarz $|u\cdot v| \le \|u\|\|v\| = 5$: a shadow cannot be longer than the arrow. The values $-5$, $0$ and $4.8$ all occur for suitable directions.

check.question: What is $|1 + e^{i\varphi}|^2$ when $\varphi = \pi/2$?
check.explanation: $|1 + e^{i\varphi}|^2 = 2 + 2\cos\varphi$, and $\cos(\pi/2) = 0$, so the value is 2. Directly: $|1 + i|^2 = 1 + 1 = 2$.

misconceptions.claim: "For complex vectors the inner product is the sum of products of entries, as for real vectors."
misconceptions.correction: Without the conjugate, $(1, i)$ would have squared length $1 + i^2 = 0$. The inner product conjugates one slot, so $\langle v, v\rangle = \sum |v_j|^2$ is positive for every nonzero $v$.

misconceptions.claim: "The overlap $\langle e_k, \psi\rangle$ is the probability of outcome $k$."
misconceptions.correction: The overlap is a complex number and can be negative or imaginary. The probability is its squared modulus $|\langle e_k, \psi\rangle|^2$, and only for a normalized $\psi$ and an orthonormal measurement basis.

misconceptions.claim: "An inner product of zero means one of the vectors is zero."
misconceptions.correction: Zero inner product means orthogonal. $(3, 4)$ and $(0.8, -0.6)$ are both nonzero and $2.4 - 2.4 = 0$.

misconceptions.claim: "Normalizing a vector changes where it points."
misconceptions.correction: Normalizing divides by the positive number $\|v\|$, which only changes the length. The arrow slides along its own line onto the unit circle.

lessons.connect: Matrices in [L3-03](#lesson-l3-03) are judged by what they do to inner products: unitary matrices are exactly those that keep every $\langle u, v\rangle$. Tensor products in [L3-04](#lesson-l3-04) multiply inner products, $\langle a\otimes b, c\otimes d\rangle = \langle a, c\rangle\langle b, d\rangle$. In Level 5 the squared overlap $|\langle e_k, \psi\rangle|^2$ becomes the Born rule for measurement probabilities.
lessons.caution: This lesson works in finite dimensions with the standard inner product on $\mathbb{C}^n$, conjugate-linear in the first slot (the physics and NumPy convention). Other inner products exist (weighted sums, integrals for functions) and obey the same three axioms. The angle $\theta$ is defined only for real vectors; for complex vectors only $|\langle u, v\rangle|$ has an angle-like meaning. Reading squared overlaps as probabilities is a postulate of quantum theory that requires a normalized state and an orthonormal measurement basis; the algebra here does not by itself say anything about experiments.

instructor.why: Students arrive with the dot product as a formula; quantum information needs it as geometry (shadows, orthogonality) and as a complex construction (the conjugate). Cauchy-Schwarz is the first real proof in the course whose idea, subtract the projection and look at what is left, recurs in Gram-Schmidt, least squares and the Born rule [@mml; @nielsenchuang].
teaching_notes: Open with the $(1, i)$ puzzle and let students propose fixes before showing the conjugate; most will try absolute values of entries, which is the right idea.
Use the projection explorer to ask for predictions: where is the shadow longest, zero, negative? Students should find $53.13^\circ$, $143.13^\circ$ and $233.13^\circ$ before moving the slider.
Spend time on the proof of Cauchy-Schwarz. Draw the projection $p$ and remainder $r$ for real vectors, then point out that the algebra never used the picture, which is why it works in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Check the conjugate convention whenever students use software: `np.dot` does not conjugate, `np.vdot` does.
instructor.assessment: The second stretch exercise (Parseval in a turned basis) and the worked example show whether students can expand in an orthonormal basis. The triangle-inequality challenge tests whether they can use Cauchy-Schwarz as a tool. The second check question catches the missing conjugate.
instructor.extend: Derive the Gram-Schmidt process: given independent $v_1, v_2$, set $e_1 = v_1/\|v_1\|$ and $e_2 = (v_2 - \langle e_1, v_2\rangle e_1)/\|\cdot\|$. Apply it to $(1, 1, 0)$ and $(1, 0, 1)$. Mathematics for Machine Learning, chapter 3, develops inner products, angles and projections in this spirit [@mml].

further.note: Chapter 3 (analytic geometry): norms, inner products, angles, orthonormal bases and projections.
Section 2.1 states the inner product conventions used from Level 5 on.

lessons.title: Matrices as transformations
lessons.objective: Read a matrix as the transformation that sends the basis vectors to its columns, compose transformations in the right order, use the determinant as signed area scaling, and test whether a matrix is unitary.
lessons.big_idea: A matrix is a recipe for moving the whole plane: its columns say where the basis vectors go, the determinant says how areas scale, and the unitary matrices are exactly the moves that keep every length and every inner product.
outcomes: Compute $Mv$ and $AB$, and explain why the columns of $M$ are $Me_0$ and $Me_1$ and why $ABv$ means: apply $B$ first, then $A$.
Compute a $2\times 2$ determinant, interpret its sign and size as orientation and area scaling, and use it to decide invertibility and write the inverse.
Form the conjugate transpose $U^\dagger$, test $U^\dagger U = I$, and prove that this is equivalent to preserving inner products and to preserving norms.

key_terms.meaning: A function $M$ with $M(av + bw) = aMv + bMw$; on $\mathbb{C}^n$ every linear map is multiplication by a matrix.
$(AB)_{jk} = \sum_m A_{jm}B_{mk}$; it is the matrix of the composite map $v \mapsto A(Bv)$.
For $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$, $ad - bc$: the signed factor by which the map scales areas.
$U^\dagger$, obtained by turning rows into columns and conjugating every entry: $(U^\dagger)_{jk} = \overline{U_{kj}}$.
A square matrix with $U^\dagger U = I$; real unitary matrices are called orthogonal.

motivation: In [L3-02](#lesson-l3-02) you measured vectors. Now we move them. A quantum gate, a rotation of a robot arm, a layer of a neural network and a change of coordinates are all the same kind of object: a rule that sends every vector to a new vector and respects addition and scaling. Such a rule is completely fixed by where it sends the basis vectors, and writing those images side by side gives a matrix.

Two questions about these moves matter for everything later. Can the move be undone? (A camera that flattens a 3-D scene into a photo cannot be undone; a rotation can.) And does it keep lengths? Quantum states must stay normalized, so the moves allowed on a closed quantum system are exactly the length-keeping ones. A tempting shortcut is to think that a matrix with determinant 1 keeps lengths because it keeps area. The shear in this lesson shows that this is false, and the theorem at the end shows what the right test is.

sections.heading: A matrix is where the basis vectors go

blocks.title: Matrix times vector
blocks.label: def-l3-03-matvec
blocks.md: For an $m\times n$ matrix $M$ and $v \in \mathbb{C}^n$, $\;(Mv)_j = \sum_{k=1}^{n} M_{jk} v_k$: each output entry is a row of $M$ times the column $v$. The number of columns of $M$ must equal the number of entries of $v$ [@openstax_matrices].

blocks.title: Columns are images of the basis
blocks.label: prop-l3-03-columns
blocks.md: The $k$-th column of $M$ is $Me_k$. Because $v = \sum_k v_k e_k$ and matrix multiplication is linear, $Mv = \sum_k v_k\,(Me_k)$: the image of any vector is the same combination of the columns.

blocks.latex: \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = x\begin{pmatrix} a \\ c \end{pmatrix} + y\begin{pmatrix} b \\ d \end{pmatrix}
blocks.label: eq-l3-03-columns

blocks.md: Equation [](#eq-l3-03-columns) is the picture to keep. Draw the grid of the plane; a matrix moves $e_0 = (1, 0)$ to its first column and $e_1 = (0, 1)$ to its second, and every grid line follows along, staying straight, parallel and evenly spaced. Four examples carry the whole lesson: the quarter turn $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, the shear $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, the reflection $F = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and the collapse $C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1/2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.alt: The whole coordinate grid with a shaded unit square is turned a quarter turn, sheared, reflected and finally collapsed onto a line, with each matrix and its determinant shown.
blocks.caption: The grid under $R$, $S$, $F$ and $C$. The shaded unit square tracks the determinant: $\det R = 1$, $\det S = 1$, $\det F = -1$, $\det C = 0$.
blocks.describe: A blue grid fills the screen with the unit square shaded and the basis vectors $e_0$ (purple) and $e_1$ (orange). A card explains that the columns of a matrix are where the basis vectors land. First the quarter turn $R$ rotates the whole grid by $90^\circ$: $e_0$ lands on $(0, 1)$ and $e_1$ on $(-1, 0)$; the card shows $\det R = 1$, area kept. The grid turns back. The shear $S$ slides each horizontal line sideways in proportion to its height, so the square becomes a parallelogram of the same area: $\det S = 1$. The reflection $F$ flips the grid in the horizontal axis; the square keeps its area but its orientation reverses: $\det F = -1$. Finally the collapse $C$ squeezes the entire plane onto the line through $(2, 1)$; the square becomes a segment of area zero, $\det C = 0$. A red arrow marks $(2, -1)$, which $C$ sends to $(0, 0)$, so no inverse can exist.

sections.heading: Composition: the order of the moves

blocks.title: Matrix product
blocks.label: def-l3-03-product
blocks.md: For an $m\times p$ matrix $A$ and a $p\times n$ matrix $B$, $(AB)_{jk} = \sum_{m'=1}^{p} A_{jm'} B_{m'k}$. Column $k$ of $AB$ is $A$ applied to column $k$ of $B$, so $(AB)v = A(Bv)$ for every $v$.

blocks.alt: The grid is sheared and then turned, giving RS; it is reset and then turned and sheared, giving SR; the basis vectors end in different places.
blocks.caption: Shear then turn ($RS$) versus turn then shear ($SR$). The final grids differ, so $RS \ne SR$.
blocks.describe: The grid with its unit square first undergoes the shear $S$ and then the quarter turn $R$. The basis vectors end at the columns of $RS = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, namely $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 1)$, which are marked with dots. The grid is reset. Now $R$ acts first and $S$ second; the basis vectors end at the columns of $SR = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, namely $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$, away from the dots. A card shows both products and the conclusion $RS \ne SR$.

blocks.md: Compute it by rows times columns: $RS = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $SR = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Matrix multiplication is associative, $(AB)C = A(BC)$, because composing functions is associative, but it is not commutative. In a quantum circuit drawn left to right, the gate drawn first is written rightmost in the product.

sections.heading: The determinant: area, orientation and undoing

blocks.title: Determinant of a two-by-two matrix
blocks.label: def-l3-03-det
blocks.md: $\det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc$.

blocks.title: Signed area scaling
blocks.label: prop-l3-03-area
blocks.md: The unit square is sent to the parallelogram spanned by the columns $(a, c)$ and $(b, d)$. Its area is $|ad - bc|$, and $ad - bc < 0$ exactly when the map reverses orientation (it turns the counterclockwise order of $e_0, e_1$ into clockwise).

Put the parallelogram with vertices $0$, $(a, c)$, $(a + b, c + d)$, $(b, d)$ into the shoelace formula: twice the signed area is $(a(c + d) - (a + b)c) + ((a + b)d - b(c + d)) = (ad - bc) + (ad - bc)$, so the signed area is $ad - bc$. Its sign is positive when $(b, d)$ lies counterclockwise from $(a, c)$, which is the orientation of $e_0, e_1$.

blocks.title: Determinants multiply; the two-by-two inverse
blocks.label: thm-l3-03-det
blocks.md: For $2\times 2$ matrices, $\det(AB) = \det A\,\det B$. A $2\times 2$ matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ is invertible exactly when $\det M \ne 0$, and then $M^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}$.

Let $B = \begin{pmatrix} e & f \\ g & h \end{pmatrix}$. Then $AB = \begin{pmatrix} ae + bg & af + bh \\ ce + dg & cf + dh \end{pmatrix}$ and $\det(AB) = (ae + bg)(cf + dh) - (af + bh)(ce + dg)$. The terms $acef$ and $bdgh$ cancel, leaving $adeh + bcfg - adfg - bceh = (ad - bc)(eh - fg)$. For the inverse, multiply: $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix} = (ad - bc)\,I$, so dividing by $ad - bc \ne 0$ gives $M^{-1}$. If $\det M = 0$ and $M^{-1}$ existed, then $1 = \det I = \det M \det M^{-1} = 0$, a contradiction.

For the four examples, $\det R = 1$, $\det S = 1$, $\det F = -1$ and $\det C = 0$. The collapse has columns $(1, 1/2)$ and $(2, 1)$, the second twice the first, so the whole plane lands on one line and $C(2, -1) = (2 - 2,\ 1 - 1) = (0, 0)$. Two different inputs, $(2, -1)$ and $(0, 0)$, have the same output, so no rule can recover the input: a zero determinant means information is lost.

blocks.caption: The same four matrices acting on the unit square (cyan), the unit circle (red) and a flag that shows orientation. Only $R$ and $F$ send the circle to itself; the shear stretches it into an ellipse even though $\det S = 1$.

blocks.alt: Side by side, a rotation by 30 degrees and the shear S act on a point moving around the unit circle; the rotated length stays 1.000 while the sheared length swings between 0.618 and 1.618.
blocks.caption: A rotation keeps every length; the shear $S$, with the same determinant 1, stretches some directions to $1.618$ and shrinks others to $0.618$.
blocks.describe: Two coordinate planes show the unit circle. On the left the rotation $R_{30}$ by $30^\circ$ maps it to itself; on the right the shear $S$ maps it to a tilted ellipse. A gray input arrow $x$ runs once around the circle, and colored arrows show $R_{30}x$ and $Sx$, with live readouts of their lengths. The rotated length stays 1.000 throughout. The sheared length varies; the animation stops at the longest image, length 1.618, and the shortest, length 0.618 (these are $(1 + \sqrt5)/2$ and its reciprocal). A final line notes that $\det S = 1$ although lengths change: keeping area is not keeping length.

blocks.title: Conjugate transpose and unitary matrix
blocks.label: def-l3-03-unitary
blocks.md: The **conjugate transpose** of a matrix $A$ is $A^\dagger$ with $(A^\dagger)_{jk} = \overline{A_{kj}}$. A square matrix $U$ is **unitary** if $U^\dagger U = I$; then $U^{-1} = U^\dagger$. A real unitary matrix is called **orthogonal** ($U^{\mathsf T} U = I$).

blocks.title: Moving a matrix across the inner product
blocks.label: lem-l3-03-adjoint
blocks.md: For every matrix $A$ and vectors $u, v$ of matching sizes, $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$.

$\langle Au, v\rangle = \sum_j \overline{(Au)_j}\,v_j = \sum_j \sum_k \overline{A_{jk}}\,\overline{u_k}\,v_j = \sum_k \overline{u_k} \sum_j (A^\dagger)_{kj} v_j = \sum_k \overline{u_k}\,(A^\dagger v)_k = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$.

blocks.title: Three equivalent descriptions of unitarity
blocks.label: thm-l3-03-unitary
blocks.md: For a square complex matrix $U$ the following are equivalent: (i) $U^\dagger U = I$; (ii) $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle$ for all $u, v$; (iii) $\|Uv\| = \|v\|$ for all $v$.

(i) implies (ii): by the lemma, $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u, U^\dagger U v\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle$. (ii) implies (iii): take $u = v$. (iii) implies (ii): the polarization identity $\langle u, v\rangle = \frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3} i^{k}\,\|i^{k}u + v\|^2$ writes every inner product through norms (expand $\|i^k u + v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(i^{-k}\langle u, v\rangle)$ and sum). Since $U(i^k u + v) = i^k Uu + Uv$, preserving all norms preserves all inner products. (ii) implies (i): the $(j, k)$ entry of $U^\dagger U$ is $\langle e_j, U^\dagger U e_k\rangle = \langle U e_j, U e_k\rangle = \langle e_j, e_k\rangle = \delta_{jk}$, which is the $(j, k)$ entry of $I$.

blocks.latex: U^\dagger U = I \iff \|Uv\| = \|v\| \text{ for every } v
blocks.label: eq-l3-03-unitary

blocks.md: Equivalently, $U$ is unitary exactly when its columns form an orthonormal basis, because the $(j, k)$ entry of $U^\dagger U$ is the inner product of column $j$ with column $k$. Check the Hadamard matrix $H = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$: its columns $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$ are the orthonormal basis $e_\pm$ of [L3-02](#lesson-l3-02). Applied to $(1, 0)$ it gives $(1/\sqrt2, 1/\sqrt2)$; applied again it gives $(1, 0)$, because $H^2 = I$. The phase matrix $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & i \end{pmatrix}$ is unitary but has no real picture as a rotation of the plane: it rotates the second complex amplitude by $90^\circ$ in its own complex plane. The shear fails the test: $S^{\mathsf T} S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \ne I$, and indeed $\|S e_1\| = \|(1, 1)\| = \sqrt2$.

blocks.caption: How the classes of matrices in this lesson nest. Unitary matrices are invertible ($U^{-1} = U^\dagger$, $|\det U| = 1$); real orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrices are rotations or reflections. The shear is invertible with determinant 1 but is not unitary.

Choose a matrix from the menu. The cyan shape is the image of the unit square, the red curve the image of the unit circle, and the arrows are the two columns. The title gives the determinant and whether all lengths are kept.
blocks.describe: A single plot shows the dotted unit square and unit circle and their images under the chosen matrix, with the columns $Me_0$ and $Me_1$ as purple and orange arrows. The menu offers the identity, a rotation by $30^\circ$, the shear $S$ (determinant 1, lengths change), the reflection $F$ (determinant $-1$, lengths kept), the collapse $C$ (determinant 0; square and circle flatten onto a line), a stretch $\operatorname{diag}(2, 1/2)$ (determinant 1, lengths change) and the Hadamard matrix $H$ (determinant $-1$, lengths kept). Only the matrices that keep lengths send the circle to itself.

blocks.title: Unitary is not the same as stochastic
blocks.md: A stochastic matrix such as $T = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$ (non-negative entries, columns summing to 1) keeps the **sum** of a probability vector: $T(0.5, 0.5) = (0.55, 0.45)$. It does not keep the length: $\|(0.5, 0.5)\| \approx 0.707$ but $\|(0.55, 0.45)\| \approx 0.711$. Unitary matrices keep the length of amplitude vectors, which is what normalization of quantum states requires. Closed quantum systems evolve by unitary matrices; measurement and noise need the more general descriptions of Level 5 [@nielsenchuang; @watrous].

blocks.explain: NumPy's `@` is the matrix product and `M.conj().T` is $M^\dagger$. The cell checks every claim of the lesson: columns, determinants, $RS \ne SR$, the inverse formula, the shear's stretch factors, unitarity tests and a stochastic matrix.
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

R = np.array([[0, -1], [1, 0]])        # quarter turn
S = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 1]])         # shear
F = np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]])        # reflection in the x axis
C = np.array([[1, 2], [0.5, 1]])       # collapse onto a line
e0, e1 = np.array([1, 0]), np.array([0, 1])

# columns are the images of the basis vectors
print('R e0 =', R @ e0, ' R e1 =', R @ e1, ' (the columns of R)')
for name, M in (('R', R), ('S', S), ('F', F), ('C', C)):
    print(f'det {name} = {np.linalg.det(M):+.3f}')
print('C (2, -1) =', C @ np.array([2, -1]), ' so C squashes a whole line to 0')

# order matters
print('RS =', (R @ S).tolist(), '  SR =', (S @ R).tolist())
v = np.array([1, 2])
assert np.allclose((R @ S) @ v, R @ (S @ v))      # RS v means: S first, then R

# 2 x 2 inverse from the determinant
A = np.array([[3, 1], [4, 2]])
Ainv = np.array([[2, -1], [-4, 3]]) / np.linalg.det(A)
print('det A =', round(np.linalg.det(A), 6), ' A^{-1} =', Ainv.tolist(), ' check', np.allclose(A @ Ainv, np.eye(2)))

# det S = 1, yet S changes lengths: singular values are the extreme stretch factors
print('|S e1| =', np.linalg.norm(S @ e1), '  singular values of S:', np.linalg.svd(S, compute_uv=False).round(3))

# unitary matrices: U^dagger U = I
H = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]]) / np.sqrt(2)
P = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1j]])
U = np.array([[1, 1j], [1j, 1]]) / np.sqrt(2)
for name, M in (('H', H), ('P', P), ('U', U), ('S', S)):
    print(name, 'unitary:', np.allclose(M.conj().T @ M, np.eye(2)), '  |det| =', round(abs(np.linalg.det(M)), 6))
print('H(1,0) =', (H @ e0).round(4), '  H H (1,0) =', (H @ H @ e0).round(10))

# a random complex vector keeps its norm under U, and inner products are kept too
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = rng.normal(size=2) + 1j * rng.normal(size=2)
y = rng.normal(size=2) + 1j * rng.normal(size=2)
print('norms:', round(np.linalg.norm(x), 6), round(np.linalg.norm(U @ x), 6),
      '  inner products equal:', np.isclose(np.vdot(U @ x, U @ y), np.vdot(x, y)))

# a stochastic matrix keeps the SUM of a probability vector, not its length
T = np.array([[0.9, 0.2], [0.1, 0.8]])
p = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
print('T p =', T @ p, ' sum', (T @ p).sum(), '  lengths', round(np.linalg.norm(p), 4), round(np.linalg.norm(T @ p), 4))

worked_example.title: A beam-splitter matrix
worked_example.problem: Let $U = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Show that $U$ is unitary, compute $U(1, 0)$ and $U(1, 1)/\sqrt2$, and find $\det U$.
steps: Conjugate transpose: transposing changes nothing here (the matrix is symmetric), and conjugating turns $i$ into $-i$, so $U^\dagger = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ -i & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Product: $U^\dagger U = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot 1 + (-i)(i) & 1\cdot i + (-i)\cdot 1 \\ (-i)\cdot 1 + 1\cdot i & (-i)(i) + 1\cdot 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = I$. So $U$ is unitary. (Equivalently its columns $(1, i)/\sqrt2$ and $(i, 1)/\sqrt2$ are orthonormal; their inner product is $\bar 1\cdot i + \bar i\cdot 1 = 0$, as in [L3-02](#lesson-l3-02).)

Images: $U(1, 0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, i)$, with squared norm $\frac12(1 + 1) = 1$. And $U\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1) = \frac12(1 + i,\ i + 1) = \frac{1 + i}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$: the input is only multiplied by the unit complex number $\frac{1 + i}{\sqrt2} = e^{i\pi/4}$, so its norm stays 1.
Determinant: $\det U = \frac12(1\cdot 1 - i\cdot i) = \frac12(1 + 1) = 1$, consistent with $|\det U| = 1$ for every unitary matrix.
worked_example.result: $U$ is unitary with $U^{-1} = U^\dagger$ and $\det U = 1$. It sends $(1, 0)$ to the equal-weight vector $(1, i)/\sqrt2$, the matrix of an ideal 50:50 beam splitter in one common convention.

exercises.prompt: Apply $H = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ to $v = (1, 0)$. Then apply $H$ once more. Check the norm after each step.
exercises.solution: $Hv = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$, with norm $\sqrt{\frac12 + \frac12} = 1$. Then $H(Hv) = \frac12(1 + 1,\ 1 - 1) = (1, 0)$: the second entry cancels. The norm is again 1, and $H^2 = I$.

exercises.prompt: Write the matrix $M$ that sends $e_0$ to $(2, 1)$ and $e_1$ to $(1, 3)$. Compute $M(1, -1)$ and $\det M$.
exercises.solution: The columns are the images: $M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $M(1, -1) = 1\cdot(2, 1) - 1\cdot(1, 3) = (1, -2)$, and $\det M = 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 1 = 5$: areas grow by a factor of 5 and orientation is kept.

exercises.prompt: Find $\det A$ and $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and check $AA^{-1} = I$.
exercises.solution: $\det A = 3\cdot 2 - 1\cdot 4 = 2$. So $A^{-1} = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1/2 \\ -2 & 3/2 \end{pmatrix}$. Check: first row of $AA^{-1}$ is $(3 - 2,\ -3/2 + 3/2) = (1, 0)$, second row is $(4 - 4,\ -2 + 3) = (0, 1)$.

exercises.prompt: Show that the shear $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is not unitary in two ways: by computing $S^{\mathsf T}S$, and by finding a unit vector whose image is longer than 1. Is $S$ invertible?
exercises.solution: $S^{\mathsf T}S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \ne I$. The unit vector $e_1$ goes to $(1, 1)$, of length $\sqrt2 > 1$. Yes, $S$ is invertible: $\det S = 1$ and $S^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ (shear back). Invertible does not imply unitary.

exercises.prompt: For $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ compute $RS$ and $SR$ and apply each to $(1, 0)$. Interpret the results as sequences of moves.
exercises.solution: $RS = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $SR = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. $RS(1, 0) = (0, 1)$: the shear leaves $(1, 0)$ alone, then the turn sends it to $(0, 1)$. $SR(1, 0) = (1, 1)$: the turn sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$, then the shear moves it to $(1, 1)$. Different order, different result.

exercises.prompt: Prove that every real $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix ($Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$) is either a rotation $\begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{pmatrix}$ (determinant 1) or a reflection $\begin{pmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \\ \sin t & -\cos t \end{pmatrix}$ (determinant $-1$).
exercises.solution: $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$ says the columns are orthonormal. The first column is a unit vector, so it equals $(\cos t, \sin t)$ for some $t$. The second column is a unit vector orthogonal to it; in the plane there are exactly two, $(-\sin t, \cos t)$ and $(\sin t, -\cos t)$. The first choice gives the rotation, with determinant $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$; the second gives the reflection, with determinant $-\cos^2 t - \sin^2 t = -1$ (it is the reflection in the line at angle $t/2$).

exercises.prompt: Show that $|\det U| = 1$ for every $2\times 2$ unitary matrix $U$. You may use $\det(AB) = \det A\det B$ and $\det(A^\dagger) = \overline{\det A}$.
exercises.solution: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$, $A^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} \bar a & \bar c \\ \bar b & \bar d \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $\bar a\bar d - \bar c\bar b = \overline{ad - bc}$, which confirms the hint. Then $1 = \det I = \det(U^\dagger U) = \det U^\dagger\,\det U = \overline{\det U}\,\det U = |\det U|^2$, so $|\det U| = 1$. Examples: $\det H = -1$, $\det P = i$, and the beam splitter has $\det U = 1$.

check.question: A matrix $M$ sends $e_0 = (1, 0)$ to $(2, 5)$ and $e_1 = (0, 1)$ to $(-1, 3)$. What is $M$?
check.explanation: The columns of $M$ are the images of the basis vectors, so $(2, 5)$ is the first column and $(-1, 3)$ the second. Writing the images as rows gives the transpose, a different map.

check.question: A $2\times 2$ real matrix has determinant $-1$. What does it do to the unit square?
options: Keeps its area and reverses its orientation
Keeps both its area and its orientation
check.explanation: $|\det| = 1$ means areas are unchanged, and a negative sign means orientation is reversed, as for the reflection $F$.

check.question: Which matrix keeps the length of every vector?
check.explanation: The Hadamard matrix has orthonormal columns, so $H^\dagger H = I$ and it keeps all lengths. The shear and the stretch have determinant 1 but change lengths; the stochastic matrix keeps sums of probability vectors, not lengths.

check.question: What is $\langle v, v\rangle$ for $v = (1, i)$?
check.explanation: $\langle v, v\rangle = \bar 1\cdot 1 + \bar i\cdot i = 1 + 1 = 2$. Without the conjugate one would get $1 + i^2 = 0$.

misconceptions.claim: "A matrix with determinant 1 keeps lengths."
misconceptions.correction: Determinant 1 means areas are kept. The shear $S$ has $\det S = 1$ but sends the unit vector $e_1$ to $(1, 1)$ of length $\sqrt2$. Lengths are kept exactly when $U^\dagger U = I$.

misconceptions.claim: "$AB$ and $BA$ are the same, as with numbers."
misconceptions.correction: Matrix products compose moves, and the order of moves matters: $RS = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ but $SR = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Also, $ABv$ applies $B$ first.

misconceptions.claim: "The product of two matrices multiplies matching entries."
misconceptions.correction: That is the entrywise (Hadamard) product, a different operation. The matrix product pairs rows of the first with columns of the second, $(AB)_{jk} = \sum_m A_{jm}B_{mk}$, because it must represent doing one map after the other.

misconceptions.claim: "A matrix with non-negative entries whose columns sum to 1 is a valid quantum gate."
misconceptions.correction: That describes a stochastic matrix, which keeps the total of a probability vector. Quantum gates must keep the length of amplitude vectors, which requires $U^\dagger U = I$; the stochastic matrix $T$ in this lesson changes lengths.

lessons.connect: Tensor products in [L3-04](#lesson-l3-04) combine matrices acting on separate systems into one matrix $A\otimes B$ on the joint system. Eigenvectors in [L3-05](#lesson-l3-05) are the directions a matrix only stretches. In Level 5 every quantum gate is a unitary matrix, and the order rule $(AB)v = A(Bv)$ is how circuits are multiplied out.
lessons.caution: This lesson uses column vectors, matrices acting from the left, and basis order $e_0, e_1$; with row vectors every product is reversed. Determinants and inverses are treated only for $2\times 2$ matrices, where the area argument can be drawn; the multiplicativity of determinants holds in every dimension, but the proof here is the $2\times 2$ computation. The equivalence of unitarity with norm preservation is for linear maps on finite-dimensional complex spaces. Unitary evolution describes closed quantum systems only; the effect of measurement or noise on a subsystem cannot be written as a single unitary matrix acting on that subsystem alone.

instructor.why: Students usually meet matrices as tables to multiply. Quantum information needs them as moves of a space, judged by what they preserve. The grid picture makes columns, composition order and determinants visible, and the shear gives a memorable counterexample that separates area preservation from length preservation [@openstax_matrices; @mml; @nielsenchuang].
teaching_notes: Before any multiplication, have students predict where $e_0$ and $e_1$ go under a quarter turn and write those images as columns; this makes the column rule a discovery rather than a convention.
Act out composition with two transparencies or two phone gestures: shear then turn versus turn then shear. Then compute $RS$ and $SR$ to confirm.
Use the interactive menu to ask which matrices keep the circle a circle; students should find that the stretch and the shear, both with determinant 1, do not.
Spend time on the polarization step of the unitarity theorem; it is the reason checking lengths alone is enough.
instructor.assessment: The second core exercise and the first check question test the column rule; the composition exercise and the misconception about $AB = BA$ test order; the shear exercise and the third check question test the difference between invertible, determinant 1 and unitary. The orthogonal-matrix challenge shows whether students can turn $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$ into geometry.
instructor.extend: Show that the $3\times 3$ determinant equals the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns, and that a rotation about the $z$ axis has determinant 1. Then prove that the product of two unitary matrices is unitary, $(UV)^\dagger(UV) = V^\dagger U^\dagger U V = I$. Mathematics for Machine Learning, chapter 2 and section 4.1, covers matrices and determinants [@mml].

lessons.title: Tensor products and joint systems
lessons.objective: Build joint vectors with the tensor product in a fixed basis order, count the dimension of a joint system, and decide with the rank test whether a joint vector or a joint probability table factors into independent parts.
lessons.big_idea: Joint systems multiply: a 2-outcome system and a 3-outcome system have 2 x 3 = 6 joint outcomes, a product vector fills that grid with products of entries, and a joint vector whose grid does not have rank 1 cannot be split into two separate parts.
outcomes: Compute $a\otimes b$ for vectors of any sizes in the order $00, 01, \dots$ and state the dimension of $\mathbb{C}^m\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$ and of $n$ qubits.
Use the rules $\langle a\otimes b, c\otimes d\rangle = \langle a, c\rangle\langle b, d\rangle$ and $(A\otimes B)(a\otimes b) = Aa\otimes Bb$ in calculations, and prove them from entries.
Decide whether a joint vector is a product by the rank of its table (for two qubits: $c_{00}c_{11} - c_{01}c_{10} = 0$), and factor it when it is.
Distinguish a correlated classical probability table from an entangled amplitude vector, and say what the table alone does not show.

key_terms.meaning: For $a \in \mathbb{C}^m$, $b \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the vector $a\otimes b \in \mathbb{C}^{mn}$ whose entry at position $(j, k)$ is $a_j b_k$, listed in the order $00, 01, \dots$
The $mn$ vectors $e_j\otimes f_k$, written $|jk\rangle$; they form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{C}^m\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$.
A joint vector that equals $a\otimes b$ for some $a$ and $b$.
A normalized joint state vector that is not a product vector for the stated split into subsystems A and B.
The number of independent columns of a matrix; a nonzero table is a product exactly when its rank is 1.

motivation: Suppose a model has one variable with 2 outcomes and another with 3. Describing them separately takes $2 + 3 = 5$ numbers. Describing them together takes $2\times 3 = 6$, one for each pair of outcomes, and the gap widens fast: ten two-outcome variables need 20 numbers separately but $2^{10} = 1024$ jointly. The extra room is where correlations live. Whether you are writing a joint probability table for a causal model or a state vector for two qubits, the joint space is built the same way, by the tensor product.

That raises the central question of this lesson: given a joint vector, can it be split into a part for each subsystem? For probabilities, splitting means independence. For quantum amplitudes, failure to split is entanglement, the resource behind teleportation and Bell tests. One algebraic test, the rank of a table, answers both. But the same test applied to different kinds of entries means different things, and keeping those meanings apart is as important as the computation.

blocks.md: Let system A have outcomes $0, 1$ and system B outcomes $0, 1, 2$. A joint outcome is a pair $jk$, and the pairs form a $2\times 3$ grid. To write a joint vector we must list the grid in a line, and every convention in this course reads it **row by row**: $00, 01, 02, 10, 11, 12$. Position $jk$ sits at index $3j + k$ (counting from 0); for two qubits the order is $00, 01, 10, 11$.

blocks.alt: A 2 by 3 grid of joint outcomes 00 to 12 is built from a 2-outcome system and a 3-outcome system, unrolled row by row into a column of six entries, followed by a bar chart of 2 to the n reaching 1024 at n equal to 10.
blocks.caption: Two outcomes times three outcomes: $2 \times 3 = 6$ joint outcomes, read row by row. With $n$ two-outcome systems the count is $2^n$.
blocks.describe: System A's outcomes 0 and 1 label the two rows of a grid and system B's outcomes 0, 1, 2 label its three columns. The six cells fill with the joint labels 00, 01, 02, 10, 11, 12, and the screen states $2 \times 3 = 6$ joint outcomes, not $2 + 3 = 5$. The cells then move one by one, row by row, into a single column of six entries, with the rule that pair $ab$ sits at position $3a + b$. Finally a bar chart shows the number of joint outcomes $2^n$ for $n = 1$ to $10$ two-outcome systems, ending at $2^{10} = 1024$.

blocks.title: Tensor product of vectors
blocks.label: def-l3-04-kron
blocks.md: For $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^m$ and $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^n$, the **tensor product** $a\otimes b \in \mathbb{C}^{mn}$ has entry $a_j b_k$ at position $nj + k$. In blocks, $a\otimes b = (a_0 b,\ a_1 b,\ \dots,\ a_{m-1} b)$. The space $\mathbb{C}^m\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$ is $\mathbb{C}^{mn}$ with this labeling of positions by pairs $(j, k)$.

blocks.title: The joint basis and the dimension count
blocks.label: prop-l3-04-basis
blocks.md: If $e_0, \dots, e_{m-1}$ and $f_0, \dots, f_{n-1}$ are the standard bases, the $mn$ vectors $e_j\otimes f_k$ are exactly the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb{C}^{mn}$ (the one with a single 1 at position $nj + k$). Hence $\dim(\mathbb{C}^m\otimes\mathbb{C}^n) = mn$, and $n$ qubits live in $(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n} = \mathbb{C}^{2^n}$.

The proof is one line: $e_j\otimes f_k$ has entry $1\cdot 1$ at position $(j, k)$ and $0$ everywhere else. The physicist's notation is $|jk\rangle = |j\rangle\otimes|k\rangle$. Exponential growth is real and practical: a state of 30 qubits has $2^{30} \approx 1.07\times 10^{9}$ complex amplitudes, 16 GiB at 16 bytes each, and every added qubit doubles it. In general a joint vector is **not** a product; only the products are cheap to store, with $m + n$ numbers instead of $mn$.

sections.heading: Filling the grid: the Kronecker product

blocks.md: Take $a = (3/5, 4/5)$ and $b = (2/3, 2/3, 1/3)$, both unit vectors. Put $a$ down the side of the $2\times 3$ grid and $b$ across the top; each cell gets the product of its row label and column label. Reading the grid row by row gives $a\otimes b = (\tfrac25, \tfrac25, \tfrac15, \tfrac{8}{15}, \tfrac{8}{15}, \tfrac{4}{15})$. The grid itself is the outer product $a\,b^{\mathsf T}$, and its second row is $\tfrac43$ times its first: every row of a product grid is a multiple of $b$.

blocks.alt: The entries of a = (3/5, 4/5) label the rows and those of b = (2/3, 2/3, 1/3) label the columns; each cell fills with the product of its labels, and the grid unrolls into the six-entry vector a tensor b with its two blocks 3/5 b and 4/5 b.
blocks.caption: Each cell is (row entry) times (column entry). Read row by row, the grid is $a\otimes b$, made of the blocks $\tfrac35 b$ and $\tfrac45 b$.
blocks.describe: The vectors $a = (\tfrac35, \tfrac45)$ and $b = (\tfrac23, \tfrac23, \tfrac13)$ appear at the top. Their entries label the rows and columns of an empty $2\times 3$ grid. One cell at a time, the row label and column label are highlighted and their product drops into the cell: $\tfrac25, \tfrac25, \tfrac15$ in the first row and $\tfrac{8}{15}, \tfrac{8}{15}, \tfrac{4}{15}$ in the second. A caption notes that the grid is $a\,b^{\mathsf T}$ and that row 2 is $\tfrac43$ times row 1. The six numbers then move, row by row, into the column vector $a\otimes b$, and two boxes mark its blocks $\tfrac35 b$ and $\tfrac45 b$. The last line checks the length: $\|a\otimes b\|^2 = \tfrac{9}{25} + \tfrac{144}{225} = 1$.

blocks.title: Rules of the tensor product
blocks.label: prop-l3-04-rules
blocks.md: For vectors and matrices of matching sizes: (i) $\otimes$ is linear in each factor, e.g. $(a + a')\otimes b = a\otimes b + a'\otimes b$ and $(sa)\otimes b = s(a\otimes b) = a\otimes(sb)$; (ii) $\langle a\otimes b, c\otimes d\rangle = \langle a, c\rangle\,\langle b, d\rangle$, so $\|a\otimes b\| = \|a\|\,\|b\|$; (iii) with $(A\otimes B)_{(j,k),(l,m)} = A_{jl}B_{km}$, $\;(A\otimes B)(a\otimes b) = (Aa)\otimes(Bb)$.

(i) is immediate from the entries $a_j b_k$. (ii): $\langle a\otimes b, c\otimes d\rangle = \sum_{j,k}\overline{a_j b_k}\,c_j d_k = \left(\sum_j \bar a_j c_j\right)\left(\sum_k \bar b_k d_k\right)$. (iii): entry $(j, k)$ of the left side is $\sum_{l,m} A_{jl}B_{km}\,a_l b_m = \left(\sum_l A_{jl}a_l\right)\left(\sum_m B_{km}b_m\right) = (Aa)_j\,(Bb)_k$, which is entry $(j, k)$ of $(Aa)\otimes(Bb)$.

blocks.caption: The Kronecker product of matrices has the same block pattern as for vectors: the $6\times 6$ matrix $A\otimes B$ is a $2\times 2$ array of blocks, and block $(j, k)$ is $A_{jk}B$. Rule (iii) says this matrix acts on product vectors one factor at a time.

blocks.title: The order of the factors matters
blocks.md: $a\otimes b$ and $b\otimes a$ contain the same numbers in different positions: $(1, 0)\otimes(0, 1) = (0, 1, 0, 0) = |01\rangle$ but $(0, 1)\otimes(1, 0) = (0, 0, 1, 0) = |10\rangle$. The first factor always labels the rows of the grid (the left digit). NumPy's `np.kron` follows the same convention.

sections.heading: Product or not: the rank test

blocks.title: Product states and entangled states
blocks.label: def-l3-04-entangled
blocks.md: A unit vector $\psi \in \mathbb{C}^m\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$ is a **product state** (for the split into A and B) if $\psi = a\otimes b$ for some $a \in \mathbb{C}^m$, $b \in \mathbb{C}^n$. Otherwise $\psi$ is **entangled**. The definition refers to a stated split; with three or more subsystems one must say which groups are being separated.

blocks.title: Rank criterion
blocks.label: thm-l3-04-rank
blocks.md: Arrange $c \in \mathbb{C}^m\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$ as the $m\times n$ table $C$ with $C_{jk} = c_{jk}$. Then $c$ is a product vector if and only if $\operatorname{rank} C \le 1$.

If $c = a\otimes b$ then $C_{jk} = a_j b_k$, so $C = a\,b^{\mathsf T}$ and every column $b_k a$ is a multiple of $a$: the rank is at most 1. Conversely, if $C = 0$ then $c = 0\otimes 0$. If $\operatorname{rank} C = 1$, all columns are multiples of one nonzero column vector $a$; write column $k$ as $b_k a$. Then $C_{jk} = a_j b_k$, that is $c = a\otimes b$ with $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{n-1})$.

blocks.title: Two qubits
blocks.label: cor-l3-04-det
blocks.md: A two-qubit vector $c = (c_{00}, c_{01}, c_{10}, c_{11})$ is a product if and only if $c_{00}c_{11} - c_{01}c_{10} = 0$, because a $2\times 2$ table has rank at most 1 exactly when its determinant is 0.

blocks.latex: c = a\otimes b \iff \det\begin{pmatrix} c_{00} & c_{01} \\ c_{10} & c_{11}\end{pmatrix} = c_{00}c_{11} - c_{01}c_{10} = 0
blocks.label: eq-l3-04-det

blocks.md: The determinant is more than a yes/no test. For a normalized two-qubit state, $2|c_{00}c_{11} - c_{01}c_{10}|$ is a standard measure of entanglement (the concurrence of a pure state); it is 0 for products and 1 for $(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt2$. [L5-04](#lesson-l5-04) returns to it.

sections.heading: Classical tables obey the same algebra

blocks.md: A joint probability table $P(a, b)$ for two random variables is also an $m\times n$ grid. The variables are **independent** exactly when $P(a, b) = p(a)\,q(b)$ for all $a, b$ [@openstax_independent]; that is, $P = p\,q^{\mathsf T}$, a rank-one table. So the rank test detects dependence too. The table $\begin{pmatrix} 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.2\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $0.06 - 0.06 = 0$ and equals the product of its marginals $(0.5, 0.5)$ and $(0.6, 0.4)$. The table $\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $\tfrac14$: the two variables always agree.
